title: A day in Pawleys Island and Litchfield
summary: Quiet beaches, a sculpture garden, marsh kayaking and a slower pace at the south end of the Strand
description: A one-day itinerary for Pawleys Island and Litchfield Beach, SC: calm beaches, Brookgreen Gardens, Huntington Beach State Park, kayaking and Lowcountry golf, with practical notes on parking and timing.
intro: The south end of the Grand Strand has a different feel from the oceanfront in Myrtle Beach. There are fewer high-rises and neon signs, more live oaks and tidal marsh, and a stronger sense of history. Pawleys Island and Litchfield Beach sit side by side along the coast of Georgetown County, and they are the right choice for a day when you want calm instead of crowds.

Allow a full day. The drive from central Myrtle Beach is usually somewhere around half an hour to forty minutes, depending on traffic on Highway 17, so an early start helps. In our directory these places are filed under the Murrells Inlet area, because that is the closest of our listed areas.

sections.h: Morning: a walk on Pawleys Island
p: Pawleys Island is one of the oldest resort areas on the East Coast. It began in the 1700s as a summer retreat for rice-plantation families who wanted to escape the heat and fevers of the inland swamps, and it has long been known for the phrase "arrogantly shabby": weathered cottages, no big hotels and a deliberately unhurried pace.

The beach itself is the main attraction. It is quiet, wide at low tide and good for long walks and shell hunting. Parking near the island is limited and rules are enforced, so look at the town's current guidance before you drive over rather than guessing at a spot. Arriving early in the morning makes this much easier.

On the mainland side of the causeway, Hammock Shops Village is home to the original rope hammock shop, a small cluster of shops that has been a stop for visitors for generations. It is a pleasant place to browse once you are done with the beach.

Litchfield Beach is a low-key beach community that takes its name from an 18th-century rice plantation. It has been developed gradually since the 1970s and is more residential and less commercial than the central Strand. That makes it a good second beach stop if you want a different stretch of sand without the crowds of the oceanfront.

If you like to cycle, the Waccamaw Neck Bikeway runs for roughly 26 miles through this area and gives a good look at the live oaks and neighborhoods. Check the current route and any closures before you set out.

Brookgreen Gardens is a short drive away and is the best single indoor-and-outdoor stop in the area. It has been a sculpture garden since 1932, with outdoor sculpture set among live oaks and formal garden paths, plus a wildlife trail and a lowcountry farm and zoo. The garden also runs seasonal events, including a holiday train display and market in the cooler months.

Plan on at least two to three hours, more if you like to read and linger. Admission tickets have historically been valid for several days in a row, which is useful if you are staying nearby and want to split the visit; confirm the current terms on the garden's own website before you buy.

sections.h: Late afternoon: Huntington Beach State Park
p: Huntington Beach State Park is directly across the highway from Brookgreen and is a good way to end the day. It combines about three miles of beach, a freshwater lake where alligators are often seen from the edge, a salt marsh and a reputation as one of the better birding spots on the coast. The park is also home to Atalaya Castle, the Moorish-style winter home of Archer and Anna Hyatt Huntington, who also created Brookgreen. You can explore it for a small additional fee on top of park entry.
Check the park's current notices before you go. The nature center's marsh boardwalk was closed for construction when we last checked, and trail conditions can change with weather and season.

sections.h: If you would rather be on the water
p: The marshes and creeks of this area are best seen from a kayak or paddleboard. Surf the Earth rents kayaks and paddleboards, offers surf lessons and has several locations in the Pawleys Island area. Black River Outdoors Center runs guided kayak tours of a blackwater cypress forest on the Waccamaw River and of the Murrells Inlet salt marsh, with naturalist-led and birding trips. Both are better booked ahead in the busy months.

This part of the coast is known for Lowcountry golf. True Blue Golf Club, a Mike Strantz design, plays across rolling terrain with live oaks, tidal creeks and salt marsh. Pawleys Plantation, a Jack Nicklaus signature course that opened in 1989, runs through maritime forest and along the marsh. Wachesaw East, a Clyde Johnston layout on a former rice plantation, has a signature 18th hole that plays around a pond. See the golf weekend itinerary if you want a longer plan.

list: Start early. Parking near Pawleys Island is the main bottleneck, and the beach is at its best in the morning.
Check opening days for each stop. Small shops and tour operators often keep shorter hours outside the summer season.
Bring water, sunscreen and bug spray in warmer months, especially for the marsh and the state park.
Dinner is easy back in Murrells Inlet, where the MarshWalk is a few minutes up the highway. See our Murrells Inlet itinerary for a longer plan there.
